name: Tennis Elbow
preview_text: The stiff pain that worsens with cold, the burning ache that feels better with ice, and the dull fatigue-related soreness each point to a different TCM pattern - and each responds ...
conventional_description: Tennis elbow, medically known as lateral epicondylitis, is a painful condition caused by overuse of the forearm muscles and tendons, particularly the extensor tendons that attach to the bony bump on the outer elbow. Repeated gripping, lifting, or twisting motions create tiny tears and degeneration in the tendon, leading to pain, tenderness, and weakness when gripping objects or even shaking hands. It’s common not only in racquet sports but also in painters, carpenters, and anyone who performs repetitive arm movements. Diagnosis is usually made through physical examination and history, without the need for imaging unless other conditions are suspected.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment typically begins with rest, ice, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs) to reduce pain and swelling. Physical therapy and specific stretching and strengthening exercises are often prescribed. A counterforce brace or strap may be used to reduce strain on the tendon. If these measures don’t help, corticosteroid injections can provide temporary relief, and shockwave therapy or platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections are sometimes offered. Surgery is considered only in persistent cases that don’t respond to conservative care.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, tennis elbow is classified as a type of Painful Obstruction (Bi Syndrome), a condition where Qi and Blood become blocked in the channels and sinews, causing pain and stiffness. The elbow is a crossroads for several major channels, including the Large Intestine, Triple Burner, and Small Intestine, all of which pass through the lateral elbow. When these channels are invaded by external pathogenic factors like Wind, Cold, Damp, or Heat-often after overuse has weakened the area-pain and inflammation follow.
But not all tennis elbow is the same. If the pain feels worse in cold, damp weather and improves with warmth, it signals a Wind-Cold-Damp pattern blocking the channels. If the elbow is hot, red, and throbbing, Damp-Heat is likely the culprit. In many people, especially those who are chronically tired or anemic, the pain is dull and worsens with fatigue-this points to Qi and Blood Deficiency, where the tendons simply aren’t getting enough nourishment. In older adults, a deeper Liver and Kidney Deficiency may underlie the problem, as these organs govern the health of sinews and bones.
This is why TCM doesn’t treat every tennis elbow the same way. A practitioner will look at the nature of your pain, your tongue, your pulse, and how the elbow responds to weather and activity to pinpoint the exact pattern. That pattern then guides the choice of acupuncture points, herbal formula, and lifestyle advice-making the treatment highly personalized.
classical_quote: 「风寒湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。」
classical_translation: "When the three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together, they combine to form Painful Obstruction (Bi) syndrome. This is the foundational concept for all Bi syndromes, including those affecting the elbow."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen (The Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine, Simple Questions)  ,  Chapter 43, Bi Lun (Discussion on Painful Obstruction) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first observes how the elbow pain behaves in different conditions. Pain that flares up in cold, damp weather or after exposure to wind points strongly toward a Wind-Cold-Damp invasion. The tongue coating will look white or slightly greasy, and the pulse at the wrist feels tight or wiry, confirming that the channels are blocked by external pathogenic factors.
If the elbow feels hot, looks red, and the pain has a burning quality, the picture shifts to Damp-Heat lodged in the channels. The tongue appears red with a yellow coating, and the pulse becomes rapid or slippery. This pattern often appears in acute flare-ups and signals that clearing heat and drying dampness is the priority, not warming the area.
When the pain is dull and nagging rather than sharp, and it gets noticeably worse after a long day or when the person is tired, Qi and Blood Deficiency is likely. The tongue is pale with a thin coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. Here the sinews are undernourished because the body lacks the resources to repair them, so the pain is less intense but harder to shake.
In older adults or very stubborn cases, a practitioner looks for signs of Liver and Kidney Deficiency. The elbow pain is often accompanied by lower back or knee soreness, and the tongue may be pale with a thin white coating, while the pulse feels thin and wiry. This deep weakness of the body’s foundation means the tendons and bones are not properly nourished, so healing is slow.

patterns.symptoms: ["Pain worsens in cold, damp weather", "Elbow stiffness and difficulty moving", "Heaviness or numbness in the forearm", "Pain relieved by warmth and gentle movement", "No redness or warmth at the elbow"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold and damp weather, Overuse or repetitive strain of the arm, Cold or raw foods, Sitting in drafts or air conditioning
patterns.better_with: Warm compress on elbow, Gentle stretching and movement, Dry, warm weather, Warm, cooked meals, Rest and avoiding overuse
patterns.why_this_happens: When the elbow is overused or left unprotected, Wind, Cold, and Damp pathogens sneak into the channels and sinews. Cold contracts the tissues and freezes the flow of Qi and Blood, while Dampness makes the area feel heavy and swollen. The result is a stiff, aching elbow that refuses to move freely, especially in chilly or wet weather.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, slightly swollen body with teeth marks and a white greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and tight (弦紧 xián jǐn) or slow (迟 chí), or soggy (濡 rú) if Dampness predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and Damp are the very pathogens that block the channels in this pattern, so cold weather, drafts, and cold foods directly worsen the stagnation, making pain flare. Overuse or repetitive gripping strains the already-compromised sinews. Warmth, in contrast, thaws the cold, opens the channels, and gets Qi and Blood moving again. Gentle movement disperses stagnation without further injury, while rest gives the tissues time to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the elbow warm and dry; wear a sleeve or use a warm compress when weather turns cold or damp. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and avoid raw, chilled, or greasy meals that create internal Dampness. Gentle daily movement and stretching keep the channels open, but rest the arm if pain flares.

patterns.symptoms: ["Burning pain", "Redness and swelling", "Hot to touch", "Worse with warmth, better with cold", "Thirst"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot packs or heat, Spicy and greasy food, Alcohol, Humidity, Overuse or repetitive strain of the arm

patterns.why_this_happens: When Damp-Heat invades or builds up in the elbow's channels, it creates an inflammatory state marked by redness, swelling, and a burning sensation. The Heat component makes the area hot and painful, while the Dampness adds heaviness and swelling. This obstruction of Qi and Blood flow leads to severe pain that worsens with pressure and warmth, and eases with cold.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat obstruction is aggravated by anything that adds more Heat or Dampness to the body, such as hot applications, spicy food, alcohol, and humid weather. Cold applications and cooling foods counteract the Heat, while rest prevents further stagnation and inflammation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which create more Damp-Heat. Eat cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and celery. Apply ice or cold compresses to the elbow for 15 minutes several times a day to reduce inflammation. Rest the elbow from repetitive gripping and lifting, but gentle stretching can help maintain mobility.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull ache at the elbow", "Worsens with fatigue or overuse", "Numbness or tingling in the forearm", "General fatigue and lack of strength", "Pale face", "Sensitivity to cold"]
patterns.worse_with: Fatigue and overexertion, Cold and damp weather, Overuse or repetitive strain of the arm, Poor diet or skipping meals, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Rest and avoiding overuse, Warm compress on elbow, Nourishing foods (bone broth, congee), Gentle stretching and movement
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Qi and Blood are insufficient, the tendons and channels around the elbow are not properly nourished. This leads to a dull, lingering ache that feels worse after activity or when you are tired. Unlike acute injuries, the pain is more of a deep weakness than a sharp sting, and the joint may feel heavy and weak.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, possibly thin with teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and weak (弱 ruò), may be slow.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overexertion and fatigue further deplete Qi and Blood, leaving sinews malnourished and more painful. Cold and dampness constrict the channels, worsening stagnation. Rest and warmth allow Qi and Blood to circulate and nourish the elbow. Nourishing foods directly build the deficient Qi and Blood, strengthening the sinews. Gentle movement prevents stiffness without draining energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broth, congee, and dark leafy greens to build Qi and Blood. Avoid overexertion and repetitive strain; gentle stretching and rest are essential. Keep the elbow warm and protected from cold drafts.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver nourishes the tendons and the Kidney governs the bones. When these organs are depleted - often from aging, chronic overwork, or long-standing illness - the sinews and bones at the elbow lose their support. This leaves the joint vulnerable to chronic, dull pain that worsens with cold or damp weather, because the underlying deficiency cannot ward off external pathogenic factors.
The pain is often accompanied by lower back and knee soreness, fatigue, and a feeling of weakness in the legs, reflecting the deeper root of the problem.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine, weak, and slow; the Chi position is particularly weak, and the left Guan may be wiry but thin.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver and Kidney deficiency leaves the tendons and bones undernourished and vulnerable to cold and damp, which contract the channels and worsen pain. Rest and warmth protect the depleted system and allow Qi and blood to nourish the elbow. Gentle movement keeps the channels open without draining energy, while cold and overuse further deplete the body's reserves.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broth, black sesame, walnuts, and goji berries to support Kidney and Liver. Avoid cold and raw foods. Keep the elbow warm and protected, especially in damp or chilly weather. Gentle stretching and strengthening exercises, like Tai Chi, can help maintain joint mobility without overstraining.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture hurt for tennis elbow?
faqs.answer: Most people feel only a brief pinch as the needle is inserted, followed by a dull ache or tingling sensation-that’s the “De Qi” response, which signals the point is activating. Acupuncture around the elbow is generally well tolerated, and many patients find the treatment relaxing. Your practitioner will adjust depth and technique to your comfort level.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: A typical course is 8-12 sessions, once or twice a week. Many people notice some relief after the first 2-3 treatments. Chronic or deficiency-based cases may require a longer course, but your practitioner will reassess progress regularly and adjust the plan accordingly.

faqs.question: Can I still play tennis or work while receiving treatment?
faqs.answer: It’s best to avoid the activities that aggravate your elbow during the initial phase of treatment. As pain subsides, your practitioner will guide you on gradually reintroducing movement and may recommend specific stretches. Continuing to overuse the tendon can slow healing, so temporary rest is essential for the best outcome.

faqs.question: Will the pain come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to address the root cause, so recurrence is less likely than with treatments that only mask pain. However, if you return to the same overuse patterns without addressing underlying deficiencies or protecting the elbow, symptoms can reappear. Your practitioner will give you self-care strategies, exercises, and dietary advice to help maintain the results long-term.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with physical therapy or painkillers?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can safely complement physical therapy and over-the-counter pain relievers. Just make sure both your TCM practitioner and your doctor know all treatments you’re receiving. If you’re taking blood thinners, some herbs may need to be avoided. Always bring a full medication list to your consultation.

faqs.question: Are there any dietary changes that can help?
faqs.answer: Yes. Generally, avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can contract the channels and worsen pain. Emphasize warm, cooked meals, and if dampness is a factor, cut back on greasy, sweet, and dairy foods. For deficiency patterns, nourishing soups and bone broths can support tendon repair. Your practitioner will give specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for tennis elbow during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is generally safe during pregnancy when performed by a qualified practitioner who avoids certain points. Herbal formulas, however, need careful selection; many herbs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Always inform your practitioner if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant so they can tailor the treatment safely.

research.title: Acupuncture for lateral elbow pain
research.description: Cochrane systematic review evaluating the effectiveness of acupuncture for lateral elbow pain (tennis elbow). The review found that acupuncture may provide short-term pain relief compared to placebo or no treatment, but the evidence was limited by small, heterogeneous studies. It highlighted the need for larger, well-designed trials.
research.periodical: Green S, Buchbinder R, Barnsley L, Hall S, White M, Smidt N, Assendelft W. Acupuncture for lateral elbow pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2002, Issue 1. Art. No.: CD003527. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD003527.

research.title: Acupuncture for lateral epicondylitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessing acupuncture for lateral epicondylitis. Results indicated that acupuncture significantly reduced pain intensity and improved functional outcomes compared to sham acupuncture and conventional therapies. The study supported acupuncture as an effective treatment option.
research.periodical: Tang H, Fan H, Chen J, et al. Acupuncture for lateral epicondylitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2015;2015:861849.

research.title: Clinical observation on Chinese herbal fumigation for external humeral epicondylitis
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 60 patients with tennis elbow comparing herbal fumigation (using Du Huo Ji Sheng Tang modified with blood-moving herbs) to topical diclofenac. The herbal group showed significantly greater reductions in pain and improvement in grip strength after four weeks.
research.periodical: Li J, Zhang W, Wang Y. Clinical observation on Chinese herbal fumigation for external humeral epicondylitis. Chinese Journal of Traditional Medical Traumatology & Orthopedics. 2018;26(3):45-47.
